title: Fluorescent END-BINDING 1b fusions alter cortical microtubule array architecture independently of pattern specification in Arabidopsis thaliana
content:
Abstract
Microtubules in flowering plants play a central role in morphogenesis by creating array patterns at the cell cortex that guide cellulose deposition into the cell wall. Fluorescent END-BINDING 1b (EB1b) fusions preferentially label growing microtubule plus-ends and are used extensively to assess microtubule growth polarity in imaging studies. Here, we use a variety of fluorescent EB1b fusion lines, shown to produce growth phenotypes, as perturbative probes to ask how changes to the plant cortical cytoskeleton affect changes in epidermal hypocotyl cells. EB1b fusion lines showed a range of gain-of-function effects on microtubule polymerization, the distribution of growing plus-ends, and axial growth phenotypes in different organs. Substantial differences in polymerization rate and plus-end density did not alter the frequency of cortical array pattern types observed in light-grown hypocotyls or prevent transverse patterning after brassinosteroid induction. Common differences were discovered in lines showing growth phenotypes for the spatial distribution of growth trajectories across the cell face, despite the absence of correlation between EB1b fusion construction and growth phenotype. We found that transitioning to a transverse pattern produced a significant and sustained downward shift in polymerization rate and plus-end density in all lines. These quantitative observations indicate that longitudinal and transverse cortical arrays exhibit distinct microtubule dynamics states and suggest that the underlying array architecture contributes to morphogenesis, independently of array pattern specification.
